explanation: Fires on a token that comes right after a complete noun phrase and starts an alternative name for it: most strongly ' (' before an acronym that abbreviates the preceding multi-word term (e.g. 'principal component analysis (' -> PCA), and also '/' joining alternatives (She/He, option/flag). Weak to moderate on ' and'/' or' coordinating nouns; non-acronym parentheses fire only weakly.

Fires on tokens inside news-style text about conflict, crime, security, politics or protest (resisting invasions, intelligence investigations, police, corruption, arms sales, anti-poverty campaigns), usually on a verb, preposition or function word partway through such a clause. Context drives it more than the token; neutral topics give little activation.

No single trigger: it fires on assorted mid-word subword pieces in many languages (Japanese, Finnish, Russian, Dutch, Italian), on the space in sports scores like '5-10 20:0', on 'aim' in 'The aim of this paper', on 'to' in 'referred to', and on 'open' in Popen. These examples share no concept I can find.

Fires on the token that comes right after a long subject noun phrase or clause ends, where the main verb or continuation begins (e.g. 'studies to predict the risk of complex diseases[ has]', 'a component[ is]', 'turned[ out]'), and on the first word of a new sentence in Danish, German, Portuguese and Spanish. Strongest when that token is a finite verb (has/is/are) following a long, complex subject.

Fires on subword fragments at the start or middle of words, especially in non-English text (German, Czech, Spanish, Finnish, Danish, French function words like 'se', 'il') and on the 'O'/'o' starting ophthalmology, oomycete and oocyte. Mostly a mid-word word-piece detector with a preference for foreign-language text; activation on whole English words is weak.

Fires where speech is being handed to someone in an interview or press setting: the colon after an interviewer's outlet name ('Wired.com:'), 'Q&A', 'questions', 'asked', and 'reporters'/'media' after 'told'/'speaking to'. Weaker on Q/A answer markers and forum separators.

Fires on a mid-word subword fragment of a rare or technical word (chemistry, anatomy, place names, surnames: 'en'antiocontrol, Pfannen'st'iel, Schleswig-H'ol'stein, hamster 'ov'ary, pulmonic 'st'enosis), usually the second piece of a word split into several pieces. Common whole words fire weakly.

Fires very consistently on '0' in '<?xml version="1.0"', and also on other tokens in code or structured technical text (Traceback, UserControl, p38, dates in RSS feeds, court-header caps). The XML version number is the main job; the rest is a loose mix of technical or boilerplate contexts.

Fires on the word 'pose' in any form (pose/poses/posing/posed), whether in the sense of posing for a photo or of posing a risk or question, and on the related word 'verse'. Weaker on 'Posey' and on letters inside uppercase acronyms (FES, OSA, PFS, FSH, OSHA, vfs).

Fires on tokens in code, data or garbled text: braces and spaces in SPARQL/JSON/C code, '<' in XML/tree listings, digits in numbers, and odd mid-word pieces in Italian verse, Finnish or OCR noise. No clear shared feature beyond loosely structured or non-prose text.

Fires on words that point ahead to content that comes next, chiefly 'following' in 'the following' (license text 'the following disclaimer', 'the following lines') and also 'below' and 'Following'. Also fires on the first word of a doc-comment or heading that introduces code ('Helper functions', 'Utility class').

A mixture: newlines after code lines or XML headers ("'
", '"?>
', ':
'), '/or' in 'and/or', 'to' in 'stand to'/'about to', 'advance' in 'Thanks in advance', and assorted mid-word pieces. No single concept unites them.

Fires on code tokens that refer back to or continue a declared structure: join aliases in SQL/LINQ ('on u.UserId equals[ urb]'), the loop variable in 'for (var i = 0;[ i]', PRIMARY[ KEY], leading spaces in column lists, and attribute names in HTML/JSON. Also fires on 'at' in Wikipedia 'Profile at <site>' link lines. Mostly a code-syntax detector.

Fires mainly at the start of a line in formulaic boilerplate: '#define' right after '#ifndef' include guards, 'No.' starting docket lines in legal captions, 'Category:' in wiki footers. It also fires on odd mid-word pieces (Ibbi, Peroxisome, synths, Finnish/Hungarian), so it is a mix.

Fires on a scattered set of tokens: the end of identifiers in Java import lines, the last pieces of proper names (Tecmo, Mackenzie, Foghat, Majors), digits in citations, postcodes and years, and function words. No coherent pattern.

Fires on words in narrative descriptions of physical actions or bodily situations, especially the token linking an action to its circumstances (when/while/as/to after a body action: 'trying to fall asleep[ when]', 'looked up from her toys[ to]'), and on action nouns like 'drive', 'gaze', 'ordered'. Context-driven; fires little outside descriptions of embodied activity.

Fires on a mixed set of tokens at odd or broken spots in text: the start of a quoted word, film cast lists ('Rosita Moreno[ as]'), non-English punctuation, all-caps exclamations, ungrammatical phrasing ('at this time[ put] forward'), and set phrases like 'no matter' or 'depending'. No single concept.

Fires on punctuation and operator tokens that join parts inside code, URLs or markup: member-access or call operators ('].', '?.', '::', ').'), '=' in query strings, '://' and '#' in URLs, '@' in emails, and '</' closing tags. Very weak on ordinary prose punctuation.

Two strands: the 'to/in' in idioms like 'something to do with' or 'nothing to do with', and mid-word pieces such as 'pan', 'cran', 'circ', 'ser' (Coursera, Pantry, panicking, transcranial). Also fires on some legal-order boilerplate. The parts look unrelated.

Fires on words about concurrency, threads and coupling, mostly in code or technical text: 'Thread' in Python/Java threading code, 'processes' in Pool, 'thread' meaning a forum thread, 'deadlocked', 'DispatchQueue', 'Channel', and also 'coupling'/'correlations' in physics. One theme of threads, concurrency and interacting systems, with some stray hits.

Fires on tokens inside LaTeX math, most strongly the closing brace '}' that ends a group (after \frac arguments, exponents, subscripts), and also on '\frac', '\in', subscript indices and '$$'. Moderate on '$' before dollar amounts in prose.
